body:
Monitoring and forecasting are different activities

Monitoring means observing and tracking conditions as they develop. Forecasting means estimating future conditions using observations, scientific understanding and suitable models. A forecast is an informed estimate, not a certainty.

Monitoring systems vary by hazard. Weather radars and satellites help observe atmospheric systems; rain gauges measure rainfall; river gauges measure water levels; and seismic instruments detect ground movement. No single instrument is suitable for every hazard.

HazardRelevant observationsPossible warning information
Heavy rain and floodingRain gauges, weather radar, river levels and rainfall forecastsExpected intense rain, rising rivers or possible inundation
CycloneSatellite observations, weather radar and atmospheric measurementsPossible track, winds, rainfall and coastal effects
HeatwaveTemperature observations and meteorological forecastsExpected dangerous heat conditions and relevant precautions
TsunamiSeismic measurements, sea-level gauges and tsunami buoysAssessment of possible tsunami effects after a potentially generating event

What is a warning threshold?

A threshold is a specified condition or level used to help determine when additional attention or action may be necessary. Examples include a river reaching a designated warning level or weather conditions meeting the criteria for a particular advisory.

Thresholds may be based on observed conditions, forecasts or a combination of both. Their values depend on the hazard, local circumstances and the responsible agency's criteria. There is no single numerical threshold that applies to every flood, cyclone or district.

Crossing a threshold may lead to closer monitoring, a revised bulletin or a higher warning level. The required public action must still be read from the applicable official warning and local instructions. A threshold is not automatically an instruction for everyone to evacuate.

From observations to an actionable warning

Warning preparation commonly involves reviewing observations, analysing likely developments, considering the potentially affected places and communicating the relevant level of danger. As fresh observations arrive, a warning may be revised, extended, reduced or withdrawn.

Lead time is the interval between receiving a useful warning and the expected hazardous impact. Greater lead time can allow more preparation, but only if the warning remains sufficiently reliable and people receive and understand it. Some hazards develop rapidly and offer limited warning time.

Hazard-based and impact-based warnings

A hazard-based message describes the expected physical event, such as heavy rain or strong winds. An impact-based warning goes further by describing the possible consequences for people, roads, services or other exposed assets. It connects the anticipated hazard with information about local exposure and vulnerability.

For example, a forecast of intense rainfall does not automatically establish that every locality will flood. An impact assessment considers whether the rainfall is likely to affect low-lying settlements, drainage systems or important routes. As with other assessments, projected impacts remain subject to uncertainty.

IMD's 4-colour warning system

The India Meteorological Department (IMD) uses a colour-coded public warning system. The colours communicate increasing levels of attention and action; they are not a classification of the physical origin of a hazard.

ColourGeneral public meaning
GreenNo warning; no special action indicated
YellowWatchful; remain aware and follow updates
OrangeAlert; be prepared to take action
RedWarning; take appropriate action

The colour should be read together with the actual bulletin, including the location, validity period, hazard and recommended precautions. It is incorrect to treat the colour alone as a complete safety instruction.

Uncertainty, missed events and false alarms

Forecasts are not perfectly certain. An anticipated event may shift location, change intensity or fail to develop as expected. A warning can also be issued for an area that ultimately experiences less severe conditions than forecast. Conversely, a hazard can occur with less warning than desired.

Public confidence is best supported when agencies issue timely updates, explain relevant uncertainty, correct information when necessary and communicate what people should do. A warning that is later reduced is not, by itself, proof that the original warning was unreasonable.

Prelims focus

  • Monitoring observes present conditions; forecasting estimates future conditions.
  • A warning threshold is a specified condition used to support warning decisions.
  • Impact-based forecasting considers likely consequences, not merely the physical hazard.
  • IMD colour meanings are Green: no warning; Yellow: watch; Orange: prepare; Red: act.
  • Warnings may change as new observations and forecasts become available.
  • Trap: A red warning does not mean the same impact is certain at every location within the warned area.

[India Meteorological Department, 'IMD@150: Major Science Innovations', section on colour-coded warnings, consulted 2 November 2026; World Meteorological Organization, 'Severe Weather Forecasting Programme', section on impact-based forecasting, consulted 2 November 2026; World Meteorological Organization, 'Early Warnings for All', Pillar 2 description, consulted 2 November 2026; INCOIS, 'Indian Tsunami Early Warning System', description of monitoring components, consulted 2 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Warnings are updated as observations and forecasts change.

title: Monitoring, Forecasting, Warning Thresholds and Impact-Based Alerts

body:
Why the last mile matters

The last mile of an early warning system is the connection between the warning service and the people who need to act. It is successful only when people at risk receive the message, understand its meaning and have a practical way to follow the recommended precautions.

A warning may be scientifically sound but ineffective if a remote settlement has weak mobile coverage, a person cannot understand the language used, or residents do not know which public source is trustworthy. Communication must therefore be considered part of risk reduction rather than a task completed merely by publishing a bulletin.

What a useful public warning communicates

An effective warning should provide enough information for the intended audience to understand the threat and act appropriately. Important elements include:

  • Hazard: The event or condition being warned about.
  • Location: The geographical area that may be affected.
  • Time: When the warning applies and when the hazard may occur.
  • Possible consequences: The main effects people should anticipate.
  • Protective action: What people should do or avoid doing.
  • Authority and updates: The issuing source and where to obtain revised information.

For instance, a rainfall warning is more useful when it identifies the affected district, the expected period, the possibility of local flooding and the need to avoid dangerous waterlogged routes. A message that merely announces heavy rain may leave essential questions unanswered.

Using several communication channels

Warnings may reach people through mobile messages, radio, television, public announcements, official websites, mobile applications and local communication networks. No single channel reaches everyone. A combination of methods reduces the danger that a power outage, network failure or lack of access to one technology will prevent the message from reaching an exposed group.

India's SACHET system, developed under the National Disaster Management Authority, uses a Common Alerting Protocol (CAP)-based approach for geographically targeted public alerts. CAP allows warning information to be distributed through different communication systems. The SACHET portal describes delivery through channels such as mobile messages, applications, browser notifications and feeds used by other information services.

Geo-targeting means directing information toward the area that may be affected. It does not guarantee that every device in that area will receive a message. Local public communication remains important.

Communication must be understandable and inclusive

Warnings should use clear, familiar language. Local-language communication is particularly important when technical terms might prevent people from understanding danger or action. Accessible formats and support from local institutions can help reach older persons, persons with disabilities and others who may have difficulty receiving or acting on a standard message.

Public awareness activities and practice exercises help people understand alerts before an emergency occurs. Community feedback can reveal whether messages were received, which instructions caused confusion and what practical barriers prevented action.

Trust and the risk of misinformation

People are more likely to follow warnings when they regard the issuing source as reliable and the guidance as relevant to their circumstances. Trust is supported by consistency, timely updates, understandable explanations and appropriate communication of uncertainty.

Unverified messages may exaggerate danger, announce false evacuation instructions or circulate outdated warnings as if they were current. People should confirm important information through authorised sources and should not forward alarming claims without verification. A warning that changes because conditions have changed should be assessed using its latest issue time and validity period.

Basic public precautions for common hazards

The appropriate action depends on the hazard and the latest official instruction. Common precautions include:

  • Flood: Avoid entering or driving through floodwater, and follow authorised instructions concerning safer areas or evacuation.
  • Cyclone: Follow official coastal and weather warnings, remain away from unsafe outdoor areas and comply with local shelter or evacuation directions.
  • Earthquake: During shaking, protect yourself using the recognised Drop, Cover and Hold On action where appropriate (drop down, protect your head and neck, take cover under a nearby sturdy table if available, and hold on until shaking stops); afterwards, avoid visibly damaged structures and follow safety guidance.
  • Tsunami: In a coastal area, treat strong or prolonged earthquake shaking and other recognised natural warning signs (such as a sudden rise or fall in sea level or a loud roar from the sea) seriously; move away from the coast toward safer high ground or inland areas as appropriate without waiting for a further message when immediate danger is evident.
  • Heatwave: Limit unnecessary exposure to severe heat, use shade and drinking water, and pay particular attention to people who may require assistance.

These are broad public precautions, not a replacement for location-specific instructions. People should follow the latest guidance from responsible authorities because conditions and safe actions vary.

Prelims focus

  • Last-mile communication means ensuring that warnings reach and are understood by people at risk.
  • A useful warning identifies hazard, area, time, possible impact and protective action.
  • Multiple communication channels improve reach and resilience.
  • CAP stands for Common Alerting Protocol.
  • SACHET supports geographically targeted, multi-channel disaster alerts in India.
  • Trap: Publication of a warning does not prove that every exposed person received it or could act on it.

[World Meteorological Organization, 'Overview of the Early Warnings for All: Executive Action Plan 2023–2027', section on dissemination, communication and preparedness, 5 May 2023; National Disaster Management Authority, SACHET National Disaster Alert Portal, 'About' and 'CAP Integrated Alert System', public site last updated 15 October 2026, consulted 2 November 2026; National Disaster Management Authority, SACHET, 'Dos and Don'ts', hazard categories, consulted 2 November 2026; U.S. Geological Survey, 'Can You Predict Earthquakes?', consulted 2 November 2026.]
